opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I don't really see it as much of a shift. It feels more like a natural continuation of the questions I've always cared about.

When I was working in reinforcement learning, one of the things that kept coming up was how much we depend on hand-designed reward functions and on huge amounts of interaction with an environment. I got really interested in whether agents could learn from observation instead, like watching videos of someone doing a task, the way people do. A lot of my work went into learning from observation and figuring out how to get useful signal from data that doesn't come with actions or rewards attached.

Once you go down that road, you end up thinking a lot about video. Video is the richest record we have of how the world works: how objects move, how people interact with things, what happens when you take an action. And if you can generate video, especially video that responds to actions or controls, you're effectively building a world model. That's something reinforcement learning researchers have wanted for a long time: a simulator you can learn from, plan in, and train agents inside.

So in my mind the two areas are converging. Video generation has made huge progress because of scale and better generative modeling, and RL has always needed better models of the environment. Working on generative video lets me tackle that from the other side. Instead of asking how an agent can act well in a world, I'm asking how we can learn the world itself from data, ideally in a way that's controllable and interactive.

The part I find most exciting is that once these models are good enough, the loop closes. You can train agents in generated environments, use agents to explore and produce new data, and keep improving both. So it doesn't feel like I left RL behind. It feels like I'm working on one of the pieces RL was missing.

r001.rationale: She describes the move as a natural continuation and says her reinforcement-learning work involved learning from observation, including watching videos of people doing tasks.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I actually don't think of it as that much of a shift, honestly. For me the through line has always been this question of how an agent can learn from unlabeled or unstructured data, and video is kind of the most abundant source of that. When I was doing more traditional RL work, I was already interested in things like learning from observation, learning from demonstrations where you don't have access to the actions, and video generation ends up being a really natural continuation of that.

If you think about something like Genie, which is the project I've been working on, the whole premise is: can you take a huge corpus of internet videos, where nobody told you what the controls were, and learn an interactive environment out of it? So you're learning a latent action space, you're learning dynamics, you're learning how the world responds when something takes an action. That's basically the ingredients of a world model, and world models have always been a big part of model-based RL. The difference now is that we're learning them at a scale that just wasn't possible a few years ago.

So I'd say the motivation didn't change, the tools did. Earlier, if you wanted an agent to learn in a new environment you had to hand-build the simulator, and that's a bottleneck. Now the idea is that the environment itself can be generated, which opens up this really exciting loop where video models become the training grounds for agents, and agents in turn can tell you what the model got wrong about the world. I find that much more interesting than video generation purely as a content tool, even though that's obviously a big part of why people care about it right now.

r001.rationale: The response describes a continuity between her RL interests and video generation, but does not say that her reinforcement-learning work already used videos.

astra-6.text:
I see a lot of continuity between the two. In reinforcement learning, you’re thinking about how an agent interacts with an environment and how its actions affect what happens next. With video generation, you’re also thinking about how things change over time—what happens next, and whether that progression makes sense.

The connection that interests me is whether video models can help us learn something about how the world works. Generating a plausible video isn’t the same as understanding the consequences of an action, but it opens up some interesting questions about what those models could contribute to learning and decision-making.

r001.rationale: The response describes a conceptual continuity between reinforcement learning and video generation, but does not say Ashley’s reinforcement-learning work already used videos.

sol-6.1.text:
I see a lot of continuity between the two. In reinforcement learning, you’re thinking about how an agent acts in an environment and how that environment changes over time. With video generation, you’re also trying to model how the world changes over time, but you’re learning from video rather than necessarily interacting with an environment.

What’s exciting to me is where those ideas meet. If you can generate what might happen next, especially conditioned on an action, you can start to use that model to reason about different possibilities. Generating a plausible video isn’t the same as learning an accurate model for decision-making, but that connection is a big part of what makes the area interesting to me.
